Theotokos (Debate)
thee-oh-TOH-kos
noun (Christology)
Greek Theotokos (God-bearer, often rendered Mother of God). The Christological title affirmed for Mary at the Council of Ephesus (431) against Nestorius, who preferred Christotokos (Christ-bearer). The debate was substantively Christological (the unity of Christ's Person), not primarily Mariological.

📖 Biblical Definition

Greek Theotokos (literally God-bearer, often rendered Mother of God); the Christological title affirmed for Mary at the Council of Ephesus (431) against Nestorius. The debate was substantively Christological, not primarily Mariological — it concerned the unity of Christ's Person, not the exaltation of Mary. Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, objected to the term Theotokos and preferred Christotokos (Christ-bearer), on the ground that Mary bore the human nature of Christ, not His divine nature (and God, being eternal, cannot be born); Nestorius's underlying Christology so divided the two natures as to imply two persons in Christ (a divine person and a human person), so that Mary bore the human person/nature but not the divine. Cyril of Alexandria and the Council of Ephesus affirmed Theotokos on the substantive Christological ground that the one Person born of Mary is the eternal Son of God: because Christ is one Person (not two), and that Person is the divine Son who took human nature, the one whom Mary bore is truly God the Son (in His incarnate state); Mary is therefore rightly called Theotokos (God-bearer) — not because she is the source of Christ's deity (she is not; the Son is eternally God) or the mother of the divine nature (the divine nature is not born), but because the one Person she bore is truly God the Son incarnate. The term affirms the unity of Christ's Person (one Person, the divine Son, born of Mary) against the Nestorian division into two persons. The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Christological point affirmed by Theotokos (the unity of Christ's Person; the one whom Mary bore is truly God the Son incarnate) while exercising appropriate Protestant caution about the term's later Mariological developments. The Reformers generally accepted the term Theotokos in its proper Christological sense (Calvin affirmed it could be used rightly, though he was wary of its potential abuse) while rejecting the Roman Catholic Marian dogmas (the immaculate conception, the assumption, the co-redemptrix and mediatrix titles) that developed around the exaltation of Mary. The substantive point is Christological: the one Person born of the virgin is the eternal Son of God; the proper use of Theotokos guards the unity of Christ's Person, not the exaltation of Mary.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Greek Theotokos (God-bearer, Mother of God); the Christological title affirmed for Mary at the Council of Ephesus (431) against Nestorius (who preferred Christotokos); the debate was substantively Christological (the unity of Christ's Person, the one born of Mary truly God the Son incarnate), not primarily Mariological.

THEOTOKOS (DEBATE), n. (Christology; Greek God-bearer, Mother of God) The Christological title affirmed for Mary at the Council of Ephesus (431) against Nestorius (who preferred Christotokos, Christ-bearer). Substantively Christological, not primarily Mariological. Nestorius objected on the ground that Mary bore Christ's human nature, not His divine; his underlying Christology so divided the two natures as to imply two persons. Cyril of Alexandria and Ephesus affirmed Theotokos because the one Person born of Mary is the eternal Son: Christ is one Person (the divine Son who took human nature), so the one Mary bore is truly God the Son incarnate — not the source of His deity, but the one Person born is God the Son. Affirms the unity of Christ's Person against Nestorian division. The Reformers accepted it in its proper Christological sense while rejecting the later Marian dogmas.

📖 Key Scripture

Luke 1:43 — "And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?"

Luke 1:35 — "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee... therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

Galatians 4:4 — "But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."

Matthew 1:23 — "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Theotokos debate was substantively Christological (the unity of Christ's Person), not primarily Mariological; the title rightly affirms that the one born of Mary is truly God the Son incarnate, but has been abused in the later Marian dogmas that exalt Mary.

The Theotokos debate must be understood as substantively Christological, not primarily Mariological — and herein lies both its proper use and its potential abuse. The original debate at Ephesus (431) concerned the unity of Christ's Person: Nestorius's preference for Christotokos over Theotokos reflected a Christology that so divided the two natures as to imply two persons in Christ (a divine person and a separate human person), so that Mary bore the human person but not God; Cyril and the Council affirmed Theotokos to defend the unity of Christ's Person (the one born of Mary is truly the eternal Son incarnate, one Person in two natures). In its proper Christological sense, Theotokos affirms a true and important point: the one whom Mary bore is truly God the Son (in His incarnate state), so that Mary is rightly the mother of the Lord (Luke 1:43, Elizabeth calls Mary the mother of my Lord). The Reformers generally accepted the term in this proper Christological sense (Calvin allowed it could be rightly used, while warning against its abuse). The abuse comes when Theotokos is detached from its Christological mooring and pressed into the service of the exaltation of Mary — the later Roman Catholic Marian dogmas (the immaculate conception of Mary, her bodily assumption, her titles as co-redemptrix and mediatrix, the devotion and prayers addressed to her) that go far beyond the biblical witness and compromise the unique mediation of Christ (1 Timothy 2:5). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds the substantive Christological point (the one born of Mary is truly God the Son incarnate; the unity of Christ's Person) while rejecting the Marian dogmas and devotion that the term has been abused to support. The proper use of Theotokos guards Christology (the unity of Christ's Person); its abuse exalts Mary beyond her biblical place.
